case_info.scenario: A 31-year-old woman was evaluated for generalized dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia, severe scoliosis, and motor development disorder that began in her childhood. Born by cesarean delivery to nonconsanguineous parents, she developed difficulties with head control, standing, and feeding at age 10 months. Subsequently, she faced progressive motor challenges (walking, speech, and swallow); contractures in her fingers, toes, wrists, and knees; and scoliosis. In adolescence, she experienced progressive stiffness, episodes of painful spasms and oculomotor crisis, and galactorrhea unrelated to childbirth in adulthood. Her symptoms worsened with age and progressed to her using a wheelchair, having difficulty in speech, and not having access to education. She had a younger brother with similar symptoms who passed away at age 20 years of unknown causes. Upon presentation at age 31 years, she was admitted to our center for further evaluation. She had thin limbs and was of standard height. The neurological and psychological examinations revealed scoliosis, contractures in her fingers and toes, carpal inversion, dysarthria, dysphagia, hypertonia, decreased tendon reflexes, absence of Babinski sign (Figure, A and B), and no psychiatric problems. Blood test results indicated hyperprolactinemia (prolactin level of 47.40 ng/mL; to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1). An electroencephalogram revealed atypical spike-slow wave synchronization in specific brain regions during sleep. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed significant global atrophy particularly in her anterior temporal, lateral, and frontal regions (Figure, C). Levodopa treatment was initiated but quickly resulted in drug-induced hyperkinesia (Video).

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.

case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. case_info.explanation: Motor developmental disorders in infancy and early childhood indicated cerebral palsy (CP). CP-associated movement disorders include spasticity, ataxia, and involuntary movements, often accompanied by sensory, cognitive, communicative, epileptic, and musculoskeletal problems.1CP screening should be prioritized in case of a family history of no genetic diseases. Diagnosing neurogenetic disorders in adulthood is a crucial first step. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of genetically heterogeneous neurodevelopmental, neurodegenerative disorders that are characterized by spasticity resulting from length-dependent damage to upper motor neurons. SPAST mutations (SPG4) are the most common cause of familial and sporadic HSP. Typically, SPG4 presents with a pure HSP phenotype, but its age at onset and severity are extremely variable. Early-onset SPG4 presents as complex HSP, with symptoms of motor and speech delays, progressive ascending spasms, dystonia, epilepsy, and autonomic dysmotility (neurogenic bladder, gastrointestinal dyskinesia).2,3This patient exhibited developmental abnormalities of movement and speech without signs of upper motor neuron lesions, and genetic testing did not reveal any HSP genes. Early-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT16) is an autosomal recessive, progressive, generalized dystonia accompanied by levodopa-naive parkinsonism. It starts in a single limb and gradually extends to the entire body, involving the central axial, orofacial, and pharyngeal muscles. DYT16 mostly starts in childhood, with delayed developmental motor and speech milestones.4This patient with dystonia and developmental delay had symptoms remarkably similar to DYT16; however, parkinsonism was not evident, and she exhibited hypersensitivity to low-dose levodopa. Additionally, no DYT16 gene was identified. Two heterozygous mutations in the tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) gene (c.739G>A; c.1071_1112del) were identified, confirming tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD), an autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder characterized by dopa-responsive dystonia, a group of dystonia syndromes resulting from impaired dopamine synthesis in the brain. TH is a key enzyme in dopamine synthesis, and TH gene mutations lead to impaired dopamine synthesis. Based on neurological features, THD can be divided into 2 types: type A, which is a progressive, hypokinetic-rigid syndrome with dystonia starting from infancy, and type B, progressive complex infantile encephalopathy, which presents with notable delayed or regressed motor development, feeding difficulties, hypotonia/hypertonia, and seizures.5Genetic testing can most reliably establish THD, other than that which is primarily diagnosed based on the symptoms and dramatic therapeutic response to low-dose levodopa. Increased serum prolactin and decreased homovanillic acid and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in cerebrospinal fluid are suggestive of THD.6,7In this patient, galactorrhea and hyperprolactinemia supported the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a lumbar puncture could not be performed due to scoliosis. There were no specific findings with brain MRI. In similar cases, previous MRI studies have demonstrated mild-moderate cerebral and/or cerebellar atrophy and mild white matter signal changes, but without abnormalities in the basal ganglia.5,8MRI exhibited extensive atrophy of the cerebral cortex and subcortex, cerebellum, and especially in the frontal lobe and anterior and lateral temporal lobes bilaterally. This finding was markedly different from the earlier studies. Levodopa is first-line treatment for THD. Patients with type A THD demonstrate marked improvement with levodopa administration while those with type B THD demonstrate hypersensitivity, resulting in levodopa-induced hyperkinesia.5,9Therefore, initially, patients should receive a low dose of levodopa split over 4 to 6 doses per day. Even so, some patients with type B THD are still unable to tolerate levodopa therapy. This patient was given a starting dose of levodopa, 50 mg (three times a day), which rapidly relieved muscle tone. However, she concurrently generated levodopa-induced hyperkinesia, which improved after halving the dose. This case highlights the clinical presentation of THD and the importance of a levodopa trial and genetic testing in any patient presenting with dystonia and a regression in motor development since childhood.
